newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela ministry OKs Cenbank debt refinance.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela ministry OKs Cenbank debt refinance.

text.p: Venezuela has agreed on the terms by which the government would refinance its $4 billion debt with the Central Bank, the Bank and Finance Ministry said in a joint release.

The debt -- which consists of 113 billion bolivars ($240 million) of bolivar denominated debt, and another $3.69 billion of dollar denominated debt -- would be paid off with publicly-issued treasury bills worth at least 0.75 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) each year.
In addition, this year "the National Executive will also pay off a special additional amount equivalent to 150 billion bolivars ($319 million)," the release said.
The remaining debt would be held by the Central Bank as a dollar-denominated mega-bond with an 18-year maturity paying interest equivalent to six month LIBOR plus 0.875 percent.
Interest payments will made be every half, with full amortization on maturity, the release added.

The treasury bills, issued by the Central Bank on behalf of the Finance Ministry and used to meet the interest payments, will be issued "according to market conditions," added the release, signed by Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar and acting Central Bank President Hugo Romero.
The bills are expected to slowly supplant Central Bank TEMs in open market operations.
The release charged the Finance Ministry with making the necessary annual budgeting provisions and agreed to resolve conflicts "to the best interests of both parties."

The debt stems from the early 1990s, when the Central Bank put up collateral for the country's Brady debt restructuring. Analysts have described its refinancing as a crucial step in Venezuela's IMF-sponsored macroeconomic stabilization plan.

First, the T-bills would add a monetary policy weapon to the Bank's currently limited arsenal. Second, it would put the Central Bank's balance sheet back in the black after a $78 million second half loss. Third, the bond's dollar denomination would remove one of the fiscal benefits of devaluation, so increasing incentives for the authorities to reform the fiscal accounts.
